summary: Gives guidance for planning how to assign IPv6 unicast addresses in a network, since IPv6 changes the address architecture and allocation policies that operators are used to. It offers recommendations and some case studies to help with deployment. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5375 gives guidance for planning the addresses of an IPv6 network. It covers the two kinds of address a network can use at its core, how to divide a prefix into subnets, why every subnet should be a /64, and how to pick the last part of an address that identifies one interface.

subtitle: How to plan IPv6 addresses, and why the subnet size and the private prefix both changed.

tldr.problem: IPv6 changes the address architecture and the allocation policies operators are used to, so an existing approach to network addressing cannot simply be carried over.
tldr.mechanism: The document separates the plan into the network level, where subnets are allocated from a prefix, and the interface level, where the last 64 bits are chosen. It gives recommendations for each, and two worked case studies.
tldr.outcome: The central recommendation is to use /64 subnets, because many IPv6 features depend on that length, and to treat the address space as something to be planned rather than conserved.

sections.title: Introduction: Why IPv6 Changes the Addressing Job
sections.content:
The IPv6 addressing architecture defines three main types of address: unicast, anycast and multicast. This document focuses on unicast addresses, for which there are two principal allocated types, Globally Unique Addresses and Unique Local IPv6 Addresses. In addition, until recently there was the experimental 6bone address space, whose use has been deprecated since June 2006.

The document covers the aspects that should be considered during IPv6 deployment when designing and planning an addressing scheme. The plan may be for an IPv6-only network or for a dual-stack infrastructure where some or all devices have addresses in both protocols. The address assignment considerations are analysed separately for the two major components of an IPv6 unicast address: network-level addressing, which is the allocation of subnets, and the interface identifier, which identifies an interface within a subnet. The document ends with two examples of deployed addressing plans, one in a service provider network and one in an enterprise network.

Several points highlight the differences an experienced IPv4 network designer should consider. IPv6 devices will more likely be multi-addressed than their IPv4 counterparts. The practically unlimited size of an IPv6 subnet, 2^64 bits, reduces the requirement to size subnets to device counts for the purposes of address conservation. The vastly increased subnet size has implications for the threat of address-based host scanning and other scanning techniques.

The document does not discuss how a site or provider should acquire its globally routable prefix, or the provider independent policy, since the observations are largely independent of whether the block is provider assigned or provider independent. It assumes that when an IPv6 network changes provider it will typically need to undergo a renumbering process. It also does not discuss implementation aspects of the transition from the now obsoleted site-local addresses to ULAs, noting that some implementations still know about site-local addresses even though they are deprecated, and do not know about ULAs even though they represent the current specification, so transitioning between the two may cause difficulties.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPv6 address plan is not the IPv4 address plan with longer numbers. Devices tend to carry several addresses, a subnet no longer has to be sized to the number of devices on it, and the sheer number of addresses in one subnet changes how scanning attacks work. This document sets out what to plan and how.

sections.title: Network-Level Addressing: Globals, ULAs and 6bone
sections.content:
The most commonly used unicast addresses are Globally Unique Addresses, and no significant considerations are needed if the organization has an address space assignment deployed through a single upstream provider. A multihomed site may deploy addresses from two or more provider-assigned ranges, and the administrator must know where and how those ranges are used. The reason for multihoming may be resilience failover, load balancing, policy-based routing, or multihoming during a renumbering event. IPv6 improves support for multi-addressed hosts through the default address selection methods of RFC 3484, so a multihomed host may have two or more addresses, one per prefix, and select source and destination addresses accordingly. Multihoming also carries operational and administrative burdens beyond choosing multiple addresses per interface.

Unique Local IPv6 Addresses have replaced the originally conceived site-local addresses. They improve on site-locals by offering a high probability of global uniqueness of the prefix used, which is beneficial when there is deliberate or accidental leakage, or when networks are merged. ULAs are akin to the private address space assigned for IPv4 networks, except that in IPv6 networks ULAs are expected to be used alongside global addresses, with ULAs used internally and globals used externally, so the use of ULAs does not imply the use of NAT.

A ULA prefix is 48 bits, a /48, the same as the currently recommended allocation for a site from the globally routable IPv6 address space. A site wishing to use ULAs can have multiple /48 prefixes, for example a /44, one /48, or a less-than-/48 prefix such as a /56 or /64, and in all cases the ULAs can be randomly chosen according to the principles in RFC 4193. With multiple prefixes, however, randomly chosen ULAs give suboptimal aggregation capabilities.

ULAs allow a fixed addressing scheme that is not affected by a change of service provider and the corresponding global addresses, so internal operation is unaffected during renumbering, but they must be used with caution. A site using ULAs may or may not also deploy global addresses. In an isolated network ULAs may be deployed alone. In a connected network that also deploys global addresses, both may be deployed so that hosts become multi-addressed, one global and one ULA, and the default address selection algorithm picks the appropriate addresses, for example selecting ULAs where both the source and destination hosts have them. Because a ULA and a global site prefix are both /48 in length, an administrator can use the same subnetting and host addressing plan for both.

One example of the problems ULAs may cause is IPv6 multicast. The default address selection algorithm prefers the ULA as the source address for IPv6 multicast streams, and this is not a valid option when sending a multicast stream to the IPv6 Internet, for two reasons: the addresses are not globally routable, so reverse path forwarding checks for such traffic will fail outside the internal network, and the traffic will likely not cross the network boundary because of multicast domain control and perimeter security policies. In principle, ULAs allow easier network mergers than RFC 1918 addresses do for IPv4, because a ULA prefix has a high probability of uniqueness if chosen as the RFC describes.

The 6bone address space was used before the Regional Internet Registries started distributing production IPv6 prefixes. The 6bone prefixes have a common first 16 bits of 3FFE::/16. That range was deprecated as of 6 June 2006 and must not be used in any new IPv6 deployment, and sites still using it should renumber to production address space.
sections.plainLanguage: At the core of a network there are two kinds of address to choose from. A global address comes from the registry and is visible on the Internet. A unique local address is chosen by the organisation, is very unlikely to clash with anyone else's, and is meant for internal use, like the private addresses of IPv4 but without needing NAT. The document also warns against the experimental 6bone range, which was withdrawn in 2006.

sections.title: Designing the Subnet Plan
sections.content:
IPv6 gives administrators a much larger address space, so the subnetting of an assigned prefix can follow various logical schemes. A plan can translate existing systems, by translating existing subnet numbers or VLAN identifiers into IPv6 subnet IDs; it can be a redesign, allocating according to need; or it can be based on aggregation. Aggregation can follow geographical boundaries, by assigning a common prefix to all subnets within an area, organisational boundaries, by assigning a common prefix to an entire organisation or group, or service type, by reserving prefixes for predefined services such as VoIP, content distribution, wireless services, Internet access and security areas. This last approach can create dependencies on IP addresses that make renumbering harder if the nodes or interfaces supporting those services are sparse within the topology.

Such plans can simplify network operations and service offerings, and simplify management and troubleshooting. A very large network would not need to consider using private address space for its infrastructure devices.

Several factors must be kept in mind. On prefix aggregation, the larger IPv6 addresses can lead to larger routing tables unless designers actively pursue aggregation, and while a service provider will enforce aggregation it is beneficial for individual organizations to observe the same principles. On network growth, the flexible allocation mechanism of RFC 3531 can be used to let the infrastructure grow in a way that is likely to preserve aggregation, leaving holes for growth. On ULA usage in large networks, a network with many sites each deploying a random /48 under fc00::/7 will have no aggregation of those prefixes, and the end result may be cumbersome, though no rule stops a large network from using a single ULA prefix for all its sites, since a ULA still provides 16 bits for internal subnetting. On compact numbering of small sites, a small site may experience an increase in prefix length when renumbering, for example from /48 to /56, so the best practice is to number subnets compactly rather than sparsely and to use low-order bits as much as possible, acting as though only a /56 is available even when a /48 is allocated; this advice does not apply to large sites with an intrinsic need for a /48. On assigning more than one /64 to a site, a small site may want to enable routing between interfaces connected to a gateway device, for example a residential gateway that receives a /48 and sits in a home with several LANs of different media types, or needs traffic segmentation; ideally residential networks would be given a /48 or /56 so that several /64 subnets could be used within the residence.

On sizing the allocation, by default a site receives a /48 prefix, though different RIR service region policies may suggest alternative defaults or let providers decide. The default provider allocation via the RIRs is currently a /32, and there are examples of allocations as large as /19 having been made from RIRs to providers. On address space conservation, some addressing schemes that facilitate aggregation and management could lead to significant numbers of addresses going unused; conservation requirements are less stringent in IPv6 but should still be observed. The proposed Host-Density value for IPv6 is 0.94, compared with 0.96 for IPv4, and with IPv6 the host density is calculated for sites, for example on the basis of a /56, instead of for addresses as with IPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan decides how a prefix is cut into subnets. It can follow what already exists, be redesigned from scratch, or be built around aggregation, where neighbouring parts of the network share a common prefix so the routing tables stay small. The document advises numbering compactly rather than sparsely, so that a site that later gets a longer prefix does not have to be renumbered, and it warns that a network with many sites each using a random unique local prefix ends up with a lot of prefixes that cannot be grouped.

sections.title: Subnet Prefix Length: Why /64
sections.content:
An important part of an IPv4 addressing plan is deciding the length of each subnet prefix. Unlike in IPv4, the IPv6 addressing architecture specifies that all subnets using Globally Unique Addresses and ULAs always have the same prefix length of 64 bits. The only exceptions are special addresses starting with the binary value 000, such as IPv4-compatible IPv6 addresses, which are largely beyond the scope of the document.

Using a subnet prefix length other than /64 will break many features of IPv6, including Neighbor Discovery, SEcure Neighbor Discovery, privacy extensions, parts of Mobile IPv6, Protocol Independent Multicast in Sparse Mode with Embedded-RP, and Site Multihoming by IPv6 Intermediation, among others. A number of other features currently in development or being proposed also rely on /64 subnet prefixes.

Nevertheless, many IPv6 implementations do not prevent an administrator from configuring a prefix length shorter or longer than 64 bits. Using prefixes shorter than /64 would rarely be useful. Some administrators have used prefixes longer than /64 for links connecting routers, usually just two routers on a point-to-point link. On links where all the addresses are assigned by manual configuration and all nodes on the link are routers known by the network, administrators do not need any of the IPv6 features that rely on /64 prefixes, so this can work. Using prefixes longer than /64 is not recommended for general use, and using them on links containing end hosts would be especially bad, because it is difficult to predict what IPv6 features the hosts will use in the future.

When using prefixes longer than /64 it is prudent to avoid certain subnet prefix values, because a number of IPv6 features use interface identifiers with a special form, such as a certain fixed value in some bit positions, and nodes that assume the prefix is /64 must not mistake the addresses in that subnet for having a special form. The list of problematic values is described in an appendix, is not exhaustive, and can be expected to grow. Using /64 subnets is strongly recommended, also for links connecting only routers, because a deployment compliant with the current IPv6 specifications cannot use other prefix lengths. The V6OPS Working Group believes that, despite the drawbacks and the potentially expensive network redesign if features relying on /64 subnets are needed later, some network administrators will use prefixes longer than /64.

Based on RFC 3177, 64 bits is the prescribed subnet prefix length to allocate to interfaces and nodes. With a /64 subnet length, the address assignment can be made by manual configuration, by DHCPv6, by stateless autoconfiguration, or by a combination of the two. RFC 3177 strongly prescribes 64-bit subnets for general usage, and stateless autoconfiguration on most link layers, including Ethernet, is only defined for 64-bit subnets.

The security considerations of the document add that it introduces no new considerations beyond those in its references, and that using subnet prefixes other than /64 breaks security mechanisms such as Cryptographically Generated Addresses and Hash-Based Addresses, making it impossible to use protocols that depend on them.
sections.plainLanguage: Every subnet should be a /64. A surprising number of IPv6 features assume exactly that length, from neighbour discovery to privacy addresses, so a different length quietly breaks them. Longer prefixes are possible on a link between two routers where everything is configured by hand, but the document recommends against it even there.

sections.title: Choosing the Interface Identifier
sections.content:
To have a complete IPv6 address, an interface must be associated with a prefix and an interface identifier. The option with the fewest caveats for the network administrator is that of EUI-64 based addresses, where the administrator allocates a valid 64-bit subnet prefix and the EUI-64 allocation procedure assigns the remaining 64 bits of the interface identifier in a stateless manner, with all the considerations for selecting a valid identifier incorporated into the method.

The main purpose of interface identifiers generated under RFC 4941 is to provide privacy to the entity using the address. There are no particular constraints on the use of IPv6 addresses with such identifiers, but there are implications to be aware of when using privacy addresses.

For the manual or dynamic options, the actual allocation is done by human intervention, and consideration needs to be given to the complete IPv6 address so that it does not overlap with any of the well-known IPv6 addresses: the Subnet Router Anycast Address, the Reserved Subnet Anycast Address, addresses used by Embedded-RP, and Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol addresses. The document does not discuss the assignment methods themselves, such as manual configuration or DHCPv6, and notes that they apply regardless of the prefix length used on the link. When using an address assigned by human intervention, it is recommended to choose IPv6 addresses that are not obvious to guess and to avoid any IPv6 addresses that embed the IPv4 addresses used in the current infrastructure. Following these two recommendations makes it harder for malicious third parties to guess targets for attack.
sections.plainLanguage: The last 64 bits of an address identify one interface. The easiest method derives them from the interface's hardware address, and the document recommends that for its fewest surprises. Addresses that people choose by hand need more care, because some patterns are reserved for particular uses and because an obvious address is an obvious target.

sections.title: Case Studies: A Campus and a Service Provider
sections.content:
The first case study is a campus network deploying IPv6 alongside IPv4, using the University of Southampton in the United Kingdom and a large department within it. The deployment spans around 1,000 hosts and over 1,500 users. The site connects to JANET, the UK academic network, through its local regional network, and JANET holds a /32 allocation from RIPE NCC. The current recommended practice is for sites to receive a /48, and Southampton has received such a prefix.

No unique local addressing is used on site. The campus is not multihomed, does not expect to change service provider, and has renumbered twice following the renumbering procedure of RFC 4192, which has proven adequate. It sees no need to deploy ULAs for network management, because there are enough IPv6 prefixes in the site allocation for the infrastructure, and it believes that the availability of ample global address space for infrastructure may be a benefit, since private address space in IPv4 sometimes creates problems. No 6bone addressing is used any more, since most transit providers began filtering such prefixes after the 2006 phaseout.

The campus has a /16 for IPv4, in principle 256 subnets of 256 addresses, but in reality subnets are sized to their hosts, for example a /26 where there are 35 hosts. That is efficient but increases the management burden when deployments change, since IPv4 subnets have to be resized even when DHCP is in use. The /48 IPv6 prefix is considerably larger, loosely equivalent to a Class A IPv4 prefix with 2^16, over 65,000, subnets, but with an effectively unlimited subnet address size of 2^64 compared with 256. The increased subnet size means /64 IPv6 prefixes can be used on all subnets without any requirement to resize them later, and the increased volume allows subnets to be allocated generously to schools and departments. Address conservation is still important but is no longer an impediment to management. The campus chose to deploy IP subnets congruently for IPv4 and IPv6, since the systems are in the same administrative domains and geography, and with congruent addressing the firewall policies are aligned at the site border. The allocation plan divides the address space per school or department, with a /56 allocated at the school level for around 30 schools, and a /56 equating to 256 /64 subnet allocations, with further /56 allocations for central IT infrastructure, the network infrastructure and server-side systems. Stateless autoconfiguration is used on most subnets, no DHCPv6 service is deployed yet beyond tests, and clients with autoconfigured addresses are added to the DNS manually.

The second case study is a service provider, assumed to operate an MPLS-based backbone with IPv6 Provider Edge Routers, to have received a /20 from its RIR, to operate its own LIR, to address its own infrastructure and to delegate prefixes to its customers. The requirements that shaped it are that the allocation schema must achieve maximal aggregation of all delegations into the single provider aggregate that is injected into the global routing table, that the schema must contain optimal flexibility for an infrastructure that changes with new customers and technologies, that the multilevel hierarchy of the provider need not all be mapped into the schema, since a flatter scheme can be better, and that provider network addressing should be decoupled from customer addressing.

The rules of thumb that came out of this are that no single plan fits all providers, that the levels of aggregation should correspond to the implemented network structure and be minimised, that the number of customer routes inside the provider network should be kept as small as possible, that the schema should provide maximal flexibility for different customer sizes and growth rates, and that a limited number of aggregation levels and aggregate sizes ease management.

In the exemplary plan, the prefixes assigned to all customers behind the same edge router are aggregated under one edge router prefix, which limits the number of labels needed for provider edge transport and gives strong label conservation. The /20 is separated into three pools: one for big customers who need prefixes larger than /48 and are connected to several points of presence, one for edge routers with direct customer connections and no aggregation area, and a larger pool for edge routers serving many customers normally connected through an aggregation network. Within each pool the delegation carries an additional buffer zone of 100-300% for future growth, so one or two extra prefix bits are reserved. Big customers receive prefixes between /32 and /48 with a 100 or 300% growth zone reserved, so a delegation of a /34 reserves the containing /32. All other, common, customers receive a /48 out of the pool of the edge router they are connected to or aggregated behind, again with a reserved growth zone.
sections.plainLanguage: The two examples show how the advice is applied. The campus takes a /48 from its national network, cuts it into /56s for each school, and uses /64s everywhere inside, because that removes any need to resize a subnet as the network changes. The provider takes a /20, splits it into three pools for different kinds of customer, aggregates every customer behind the same edge router under one prefix, and reserves spare bits in each delegation so that a customer can grow without being renumbered.

viz.caption: THE THREE KINDS OF ADDRESS AT THE NETWORK LEVEL

items.title: Globally unique addresses
items.text: The normal choice. Registered and visible on the Internet. Needs thought when a site is multihomed across providers.

items.title: Unique local addresses
items.text: A /48 chosen by the organisation, used inside the network. Does not imply NAT, and it survives a change of provider.

items.title: 6bone
items.text: The experimental range 3FFE::/16, deprecated as of 6 June 2006 and not to be used in new deployments.
